evidence_quotes.quote: Services such as water, electricity, sanitation, and refuse collection were not adequately provided during the pandemic.
The lack of revenue collection was predominately a result of government regulations such as lockdown, as many municipalities were not able to collect rates and taxes for the services.
The table shows the relationship between the COVID-19 pandemic and the need for governance change. The table shows a significant statistical relationship between COVID-19 and governance.

This paper followed a quantitative research approach for the purposes of data collection and analysis. the paper used a questionnaire to collect data from 449 households in Lepelle-Nkumpi municipality using systematic sampling method based on a specific equal interval starting with a random selection of the population
The respondents were asked to indicate whether the municipality was able to adequately provide water during the COVID-19 pandemic.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household perceptions of municipal water and sanitation service provision (alongside electricity and refuse collection) in Lepelle-Nkumpi Local Municipality.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2 because it discusses COVID-19 disaster management/lockdown regulations and tests municipal financial resources, ICT use, and perceived need for municipal governance change during the pandemic. However, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because the primary exposure analysed in relation to water and sanitation delivery is the COVID-19 pandemic crisis itself, along with generic municipal operational capacity, budget constraints, ICT, and unanalysed macro-governance change, rather than a specific rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household water or sanitation access (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, tariffs/disconnection rules, administrative burden, or utility regulatory structure).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data from a quantitative questionnaire survey of 449 systematically sampled households (with descriptive statistics, Chi-square tests, and correlation analyses, alongside brief references to focus group and key informant findings).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household Likert-scale outcomes on the perceived adequacy/availability of municipal water supply and sanitation service provision during the COVID-19 pandemic (Statements B1 and B4; Tables 1, 2, and 5).
criterion_notes.c5: Population (449 households in selected wards of Lepelle-Nkumpi Local Municipality), exposure (COVID-19 pandemic and associated municipal operational/macro-governance context), outcome (perceived adequacy of municipal water and sanitation provision), and study design (cross-sectional quantitative household survey) are identifiable.

study_design: Cross-sectional quantitative household survey (questionnaire with descriptive statistics, Chi-square, and correlation analysis; also mentions qualitative focus group/key informant findings)
population_and_sample: 449 households in selected wards of Lepelle-Nkumpi Local Municipality, Limpopo Province, South Africa, selected via systematic sampling
exposure: COVID-19 pandemic crisis (with general discussion of national lockdown restrictions, municipal budget strain, ICT use, and generic need for municipal governance change)
outcome: Household Likert-scale perceptions of the adequacy of municipal sanitation, water, electricity, and refuse removal service provision during the COVID-19 pandemic
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While this empirical household survey (n=449) measures perceived adequacy of municipal water and sanitation provision in Lepelle-Nkumpi Local Municipality during COVID-19, the exposure examined in relation to service access is the COVID-19 pandemic shock and generic municipal operational/financial/ICT/governance challenges rather than a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household water or sanitation access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included due to its examination of municipal governance change, financial/ICT capacity, and COVID-19 disaster regulations.
